## QUESTION 1

__Write an SQL query that provides playerID, yearID, and batting average for players with at least 1 at bat that year. Sort the table from highest batting average to lowest, and then by playerid alphabetically. Show the top 5 results in your report.__

The top five single‑season batting averages with only 1 at‑bat are all 1.000 (a perfect 100% hit rate), which makes sense because a player with a single hit in one at‑bat will have a perfect average. These players likely had very limited playing time that year.

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here

# The code below can serve as a template for all the rest of your queries. It is just missing the
# SQL code. Put your SQL query in between the triple quotation marks to create the query. The records will be stored in 'results', which is a polars data frame

q1 = """
SELECT 
    playerID, 
    yearID, 
    CAST(H AS REAL) / AB AS batting_average
FROM batting
WHERE AB >= 1
ORDER BY batting_average DESC, playerID ASC
LIMIT 5
"""
results1 = pl.read_database(q1, con)
results1

```


## QUESTION 2

__Use the same query as above, but only include players with at least 10 at bats that year. Print the top 5 results.__  

With at least 10 at‑bats, the highest averages still hover around .600–.700, but they now represent a more sustained performance over a handful of games. The names that appear are still often part‑time players or late‑season call‑ups.

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
q2 = """
SELECT 
    playerID, 
    yearID, 
    CAST(H AS REAL) / AB AS batting_average
FROM batting
WHERE AB >= 10
ORDER BY batting_average DESC, playerID ASC
LIMIT 5
"""
results2 = pl.read_database(q2, con)
results2

```


## QUESTION 3

__Now modify the SQL query to calculate the batting average for players over their entire careers (all years combined). Only include players with at least 100 at bats over their entire career, and print the top 5 results.__

The career leaders with at least 100 at‑bats show more realistic Hall‑of‑Fame‑type numbers, with averages in the .350–.370 range. These players sustained excellence over many seasons and are typically the game’s legends. The inclusion of total hits and at‑bats confirms they had substantial playing time, not just a brief hot streak.

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
q3 = """
SELECT 
    playerID, 
    SUM(H) AS total_hits, 
    SUM(AB) AS total_atbats,
    CAST(SUM(H) AS REAL) / SUM(AB) AS career_batting_average
FROM batting
GROUP BY playerID
HAVING SUM(AB) >= 100
ORDER BY career_batting_average DESC, playerID ASC
LIMIT 5
"""
results3 = pl.read_database(q3, con)
results3

```
